title: Physical Design Automation for Planar Superconducting Quantum Chips
authors: Michael Feldmeier, Marcel Walter, Gerhard B. P. Huber, Anirban Bhattacharjee, Stefan Filipp, Robert Wille
abstract: Superconducting circuits have emerged as one of the most promising and scalable platforms for quantum com- puting, with substantial industrial adoption driving qubit counts steadily upward. Yet the layout of the corresponding chips is still primarily performed manually, consuming multiple days or weeks of expert effort, even for moderately sized designs. Existing automation approaches sidestep this bottleneck by simplifying the underlying problem and relaxing physical constraints. Therefore, they fall short of fabrication-ready results. To overcome this scalability wall without such compromises, we first introduce a formal abstraction that translates physical device characteristics into a rigorous geometric problem formulation. This abstraction bridges physical realization and design automation. Building upon this abstraction, we then propose a three-stage design automation flow comprising geometry-aware global partitioning, ILP-based port assignment, and a hierarchical routing pipeline. Evaluations conducted by our interdisciplinary team of design au- tomation researchers and superconducting hardware experts con- firm that the resulting flow produces complete, manufacturing- ready layouts that comply with the physical design rules at the push of a button. That is, it operates fully automatically within seconds to a few minutes, and solves complex instances up to 25x faster than the state of the art. All methods are released as the fully open-source tool mqt-scpd as part of the Munich Quantum Toolkit, providing the first readily usable, end- to-end design flow for planar superconducting quantum chips that explicitly addresses the underlying physical characteristics and requirements.
summary: This paper tackles the critical engineering bottleneck of manually designing superconducting quantum chips. The authors introduce a novel, formal geometric abstraction and a three-stage automated design flow to solve this. The resulting open-source tool generates complete, manufacturable chip layouts rapidly, enabling the scaling of quantum processors.
main_problem: The manual layout of superconducting quantum chips is a major bottleneck, making scaling difficult and time-consuming.
main_result: The authors propose and demonstrate an end-to-end, fully automatic design flow that generates manufacturing-ready layouts for superconducting quantum chips up to 69 qubits, achieving speedups up to 25x over state-of-the-art methods.
method: The approach involves creating a formal geometric abstraction that translates physical device characteristics into a rigorous problem formulation, followed by a three-stage automated flow: global partitioning, ILP-based port assignment, and hierarchical routing.
model_or_system: The system is planar superconducting quantum chips (SCQC) containing qubits, couplers, and launchers, which are patterned lithographically. The design is modeled as a geometric composition of components, governed by physical constraints like minimum bending radii and crosstalk separation.
key_observables: Manufacturing-ready layouts, execution times (seconds to minutes), minimum wire clearance (e.g., 185 µm), and successful routing of complex connectivity.
important_parameters: Operating frequencies (4 GHz to 8 GHz), cryogenic temperatures (10 mK to 20 mK), and impedance (50 Ω for CPWs).
main_assumptions: The primary focus is on the geometric abstraction and automated flow, assuming that the initial placement of components is valid; the flow is designed for planar architectures, though the abstraction is extensible.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the SCQC layout architecture, detailing component types (qubits, couplers, launchers) and showing the abstracted representations of small and medium-sized quantum chip layouts.
paper_structure: The paper identifies the manual layout bottleneck, introduces a formal geometric abstraction bridging physics and automation, details the three-stage design flow (partitioning, port assignment, routing), and validates the flow with performance comparisons against prior art.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenge of scaling quantum hardware, which is crucial for realizing complex quantum algorithms and large-scale quantum computation architectures.

Existing approaches consider point-to-point assignments for q + 2r wires Wp distributed across r rows. The flow proposed in this work solves assignments for q + c control wires Wp as well as q resonator wires Wr and feedline connections for approximately ⌈q/rutil⌉qubits. As a result, the problem involves ordered port assignments rather than point-to-point mappings alone. Assignment optimization further incorporates wirelength and bridge minimization objectives.
